claim: Healthcare providers often underestimate patients' pain, sometimes even when aware of their reports.
source: Healthcare providers often underestimate patients' pain, sometimes even when aware of their reports.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Medical training affected the sensitivity to pain faces, shown by lower ratings.
source: We found that medical training affected the sensitivity to pain faces, an effect shown by the lower ratings and highlighted by a decrease in neural response of the insula and cingulate cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study showing behavioral ratings differences.

claim: Medical training decreased neural response in the insula and cingulate cortex to pain faces.
source: We found that medical training affected the sensitivity to pain faces, an effect shown by the lower ratings and highlighted by a decrease in neural response of the insula and cingulate cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2.

claim: Distrust toward the expressions' authenticity affected the processing of feedbacks by decreasing activity in the ventral striatum when patients' self-reports matched participants' evaluations.
source: Instead, distrust toward the expressions' authenticity affected the processing of feedbacks, by decreasing activity in the ventral striatum whenever patients' self-reports matched participants' evaluations, and by promoting strong reliance on the opinion of other doctors.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data showing ventral striatum activity modulated by distrust.

claim: Distrust promoted strong reliance on the opinion of other doctors.
source: Instead, distrust toward the expressions' authenticity affected the processing of feedbacks, by decreasing activity in the ventral striatum whenever patients' self-reports matched participants' evaluations, and by promoting strong reliance on the opinion of other doctors.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing adjustment toward MPs feedback.

claim: Healthcare providers systematically underestimate patients' pain.
source: As such, healthcare providers systematically underestimate patients' pain (Davoudi et al., 2008; Duignan and Dunn, 2008; Kappesser et al., 2006; Puntillo et al., 2003; Teske et al., 1983), a phenomenon which emerges as early as during university (Xie et al., 2018), becomes more pronounced with long-lasting experience in the field (Choinière et al., 1990; Davoudi et al., 2008), and affects prevalently women (Greenwood et al., 2018) and ethnical minorities (Ghoshal et al., 2020; Kaseweter et al., 2012; Todd et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Pain underestimation emerges as early as during university.
source: As such, healthcare providers systematically underestimate patients' pain (Davoudi et al., 2008; Duignan and Dunn, 2008; Kappesser et al., 2006; Puntillo et al., 2003; Teske et al., 1983), a phenomenon which emerges as early as during university (Xie et al., 2018), becomes more pronounced with long-lasting experience in the field (Choinière et al., 1990; Davoudi et al., 2008), and affects prevalently women (Greenwood et al., 2018) and ethnical minorities (Ghoshal et al., 2020; Kaseweter et al., 2012; Todd et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xie et al., 2018.

claim: Pain underestimation becomes more pronounced with long-lasting experience in the field.
source: As such, healthcare providers systematically underestimate patients' pain (Davoudi et al., 2008; Duignan and Dunn, 2008; Kappesser et al., 2006; Puntillo et al., 2003; Teske et al., 1983), a phenomenon which emerges as early as during university (Xie et al., 2018), becomes more pronounced with long-lasting experience in the field (Choinière et al., 1990; Davoudi et al., 2008), and affects prevalently women (Greenwood et al., 2018) and ethnical minorities (Ghoshal et al., 2020; Kaseweter et al., 2012; Todd et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choinière et al., 1990 and Davoudi et al., 2008.

claim: Pain underestimation affects prevalently women.
source: As such, healthcare providers systematically underestimate patients' pain (Davoudi et al., 2008; Duignan and Dunn, 2008; Kappesser et al., 2006; Puntillo et al., 2003; Teske et al., 1983), a phenomenon which emerges as early as during university (Xie et al., 2018), becomes more pronounced with long-lasting experience in the field (Choinière et al., 1990; Davoudi et al., 2008), and affects prevalently women (Greenwood et al., 2018) and ethnical minorities (Ghoshal et al., 2020; Kaseweter et al., 2012; Todd et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Greenwood et al., 2018.

claim: Pain underestimation affects prevalently ethnical minorities.
source: As such, healthcare providers systematically underestimate patients' pain (Davoudi et al., 2008; Duignan and Dunn, 2008; Kappesser et al., 2006; Puntillo et al., 2003; Teske et al., 1983), a phenomenon which emerges as early as during university (Xie et al., 2018), becomes more pronounced with long-lasting experience in the field (Choinière et al., 1990; Davoudi et al., 2008), and affects prevalently women (Greenwood et al., 2018) and ethnical minorities (Ghoshal et al., 2020; Kaseweter et al., 2012; Todd et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ghoshal et al., 2020; Kaseweter et al., 2012; Todd et al., 2000.

claim: Healthcare providers could have progressively changed their frame of reference of what characterizes extreme pain due to daily exposure to severe conditions.
source: Indeed, due to their daily exposure to the severe conditions, often characterized by high levels of suffering, healthcare providers could have progressively changed their frame of reference of what characterizes an extreme pain (Bergh and Sjöström, 1999).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation supported by citation.

claim: The anterior insula (AI) and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) are implicated in processing other people's pain.
source: Within this framework, neuroimaging literature repeatedly implicated brain regions, such as the anterior insula (AI) and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) in processing other people's pain (Ding et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2011; Jauniaux et al., 2019; Kogler et al., 2020; Lamm et al., 2011; Timmers et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neuroimaging literature.

claim: The AI-dACC network is partly common to that involved in first-hand pain.
source: As this network is partly common to that involved in first-hand pain (Corradi-Dell'Acqua et al., 2016; Corradi-Dell'Acqua et al., 2011; Kogler et al., 2020; Lamm et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2020), scholars interpreted this activations in terms of empathy, whereby individuals simulate the observed state on oneself (Bernhardt and Singer, 2012; Lamm et al., 2019; Stietz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Expert medical practitioners exhibited lower neural response in AI and dACC regions.
source: Critically, expert medical practitioners exhibited lower neural response in these regions (Cheng et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2007), whereas they appear to over-recruit prefrontal structures, often implicated in regulation and control (Cheng et al., 2007), possibly reflecting enhanced ability at regulating their primary empathetic responses to the sight of people potential sufferance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2017 and 2007.

claim: Expert medical practitioners over-recruit prefrontal structures often implicated in regulation and control.
source: Critically, expert medical practitioners exhibited lower neural response in these regions (Cheng et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2007), whereas they appear to over-recruit prefrontal structures, often implicated in regulation and control (Cheng et al., 2007), possibly reflecting enhanced ability at regulating their primary empathetic responses to the sight of people potential sufferance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2007.

claim: Acknowledging high levels of pain often leads to the prescription of strong analgesics with contraindications for patients' health.
source: In clinical settings, acknowledging high levels of pain often leads to the prescription of strong analgesics, which however have contraindications for patients' health (Buckeridge et al., 2010; Butler et al., 2016; Makris et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Concerns for side-effects (e.g. opiophobia) contribute to inadequate pain treatment in medical settings.
source: Concerns for such side-effects (e.g. opiophobia) contribute to inadequate pain treatment in medical settings (Bennett and Carr, 2002; Bertrand et al., 2021; Corradi-Dell'Acqua et al., 2019), as healthcare providers prioritize those cases in which pain is unequivocally established.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Doctors and nurses tended to underestimate pain in larger extent when presented with cues that patients might have lied or exaggerate their ratings.
source: In this perspective, one study showed that doctors and nurses tended to underestimate pain in larger extent when presented with cues that patients might have lied or exaggerate their ratings (Kappesser et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kappesser et al., 2006.

claim: Emergency nurses tend to privilege their own personal judgments rather than patients pain-ratings.
source: In a similar vein, recent qualitative investigations revealed that emergency nurses tend to privilege their own personal judgments rather than patients pain-ratings (Johannessen, 2019; Vuille et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to qualitative studies.

claim: When clinical assessment is inconsistent with self-reports, nurses try to convince patients to reappraise their pain or mark their own point of view in the clinical chart.
source: Furthermore, when their clinical assessment is inconsistent with the self-reports (e.g. patients denounce high suffering while few minutes before they were chatting/laughing), nurses try to convince patients to reappraise their pain, or at least mark their own point of view in the clinical chart when transferring the case to a colleague (Vuille et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vuille et al., 2018.

claim: When unexpectedly requested to repeat the task, participants reappraised each face consistently with the feedback received in the social influence paradigm.
source: Critically, when unexpectedly requested to repeat the task, participants reappraised each face consistently with the feedback received.
evidence: This claim describes findings from Klucharev et al., 2009 paradigm.

claim: Large discrepancy with others' evaluations increased neural activity in the dorsal-posterior portion of the medial prefrontal cortex (dpMPFC).
source: Furthermore, a large discrepancy with others' evaluations increased the neural activity in the dorsal-posterior portion of the medial prefrontal cortex (dpMPFC), often implicated in prediction error, whereas agreement with these feedbacks recruited the reward system in the ventral striatum (VS) (Klucharev et al., 2009, see also Wu et al., 2016 as meta-analysis).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klucharev et al., 2009 and Wu et al., 2016.

claim: Agreement with feedbacks recruited the reward system in the ventral striatum (VS).
source: Furthermore, a large discrepancy with others' evaluations increased the neural activity in the dorsal-posterior portion of the medial prefrontal cortex (dpMPFC), often implicated in prediction error, whereas agreement with these feedbacks recruited the reward system in the ventral striatum (VS) (Klucharev et al., 2009, see also Wu et al., 2016 as meta-analysis).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klucharev et al., 2009 and Wu et al., 2016.

claim: Experienced Medical Students (EMS) displayed higher IAT D-scores relative to Controls and less experienced students.
source: An Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) aimed at testing for group differences revealed higher D-scores in EMS, relative to Controls and less experienced students (see Figure 2A; see also Figure 2D for a similar effect in subjects from Experiment 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Pilot 1 and displayed in Figure 2A.

claim: Young Medical Students (YMS) were associated with higher pain ratings than both Controls and EMS.
source: Post-hoc t-tests showed that YMS were associated with higher ratings than both Controls (t(58) = 2.55; p=0.013) and EMS (t(58) = 2.79; p=0.007, see Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 1.

claim: Female subjects provided more pronounced pain ratings than male subjects.
source: We also found an effect of Gender (F(1,114) = 5.58; p=0.020), reflecting more pronounced ratings in female, relative to male, subjects (Age: F(1,114) = 1.27; p=0.271).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 1.

claim: The pain ratings from Experiment 2 did not change as function of Group.
source: The pain ratings from this experiment did not change as function of Group (F(1,48) = 0.84; p=0.369; all other effects F < 1.36; p>0.249, Figure 2E), consistently with Experiment one when the same groups were compared (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2.

claim: A positive linear relationship was found between pain ratings and neural activity at the level of amygdala extending to the periaqueductal grey (PAG) and fusiform gyrus.
source: We first tested the main effect (activations common to both groups) and found a positive linear relationship at the level of amygdala extending to the periaqueductal grey (PAG), and to the fusiform gyrus (Figure 3, green blobs).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2 displayed in Figure 3.

claim: The left anterior insula (AI) showed positive linear relationship with pain ratings under small volume correction.
source: Furthermore, when applying small volume correction in regions previously implicated in paradigms for pain empathy (Kogler et al., 2020, see methods) the left anterior insula (AI) was also found (see Appendix 1—table 3 for full details).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2 with small volume correction.

claim: Controls showed stronger modulations than EMS in the dorsal portion of the anterior cingulate cortex (dACC).
source: Subsequently, we analyzed group differences. We found stronger modulations in Controls as opposed to EMS in the dorsal portion of the anterior cingulate cortex (dACC).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2 displayed in Figure 3.

claim: Controls showed stronger modulations than EMS in the left ventral AI under small volume correction.
source: Under small volume correction, we also implicated the left ventral AI (Figure 3, red blobs).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2 displayed in Figure 3.

claim: Distrust influenced pain ratings only in Experiment 1.
source: Behavioral results were not systematic across experiments, with Distrust influencing only Experiment 1 (Exp 1: b = −0.31, F(1,113) = 5.50, p=0.021; b = 0.02, F(1,44) = 0.02, p=0.884), and perspective rating scores only Experiment 2 (Exp 1: b = 0.02, F(1,116) = 0.60, p=0.442; Exp 2: b = 0.07, F(1,46) = 4.06, p=0.0497; all other covariates F < 2.38, p>0.123).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Perspective rating scores influenced pain ratings only in Experiment 2.
source: Behavioral results were not systematic across experiments, with Distrust influencing only Experiment 1 (Exp 1: b = −0.31, F(1,113) = 5.50, p=0.021; b = 0.02, F(1,44) = 0.02, p=0.884), and perspective rating scores only Experiment 2 (Exp 1: b = 0.02, F(1,116) = 0.60, p=0.442; Exp 2: b = 0.07, F(1,46) = 4.06, p=0.0497; all other covariates F < 2.38, p>0.123).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: In both experiments, the analysis of Reappraisal revealed a main effect of both Target and MPs feedbacks.
source: In both experiments, the analysis of Reappraisal revealed a main effect of both Target (Exp 1: b = 0.13, F(1,67.99) = 52.63, p < 0.001; Exp 2: b = 0.07, F(1,32.43) = 5.70, p = 0.022) and MPs (Exp 1: b = 0.12, F(1,116.87) = 19.40, p < 0.001; Exp 2: b = 0.11, F(1,53.92) = 11.57, p < 0.001) feedbacks.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from both experiments.

claim: When each feedback was higher than participants' initial evaluation, a positive adjustment was observed.
source: Figure 4 shows Reappraisal values across three relative feedback positions on the scale. When each feedback was higher than participants' initial evaluation, a positive adjustment was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data displayed in Figure 4.

claim: Brain activity showed discrepancy effects in a widespread network involving dpMPFC and right AI extending to inferior frontal gyrus (IFG).
source: Within this framework, discrepancy effects were found in a widespread network involving dpMPFC and right AI extending to inferior frontal gyrus (IFG; see Figure 5A, white overlapping blobs).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2 displayed in Figure 5A.

claim: The discrepancy network was recruited for both kinds of feedback (Target, MPs).
source: Importantly, this network was highly reminiscent with previous studies testing deviation effects of social influence on subjective evaluations (Klucharev et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2016) (see Appendix 1—figure 1), and appeared recruited for both kinds of feedback (Target, MPs).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2.

claim: For both the Target and the MPs, agreement effects were found in a widespread network which converged around the bilateral parietal and ventral occipital cortex.
source: For both the Target and the MPs, we found a widespread network which converged around the bilateral parietal and ventral occipital cortex (see Figure 5B, white overlapping blobs).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2 displayed in Figure 5B.

claim: For the Target feedback only, the ventral striatum (VS) and the Putamen showed agreement effects.
source: Critically, for the Target feedback only, the ventral striatum (VS) and the Putamen were also found in line with previous observations (Klucharev et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2016). These regions, however, were not observed for MPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2 displayed in Figure 5B.

claim: The VS/Putamen showed stronger agreement-related activity for the Target than for MPs.
source: Finally, when testing the differential contrast Target >MPs, we confirmed an effect of the VS/Putamen in the direction of a stronger agreement-related activity for the Target (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2 displayed in Figure 5C.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants most doubtful about the pain's authenticity adjusted their response more strongly toward MPs.
source: Figure 3B displays individual effects of MPs feedback on Reappraisal (obtained from a linear model fitted on each subject individually) increasing linearly with Distrust, thus suggesting that participants adjusted more their evaluation toward the physicians' feedback, the more they were suspicious on the expression's authenticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from Experiment 1 displayed in Figure 4B.

claim: Distrust influenced how the Ventral Striatum (VS) responded to feedback agreement.
source: Interestingly, however, the analysis of the neural activity in Experiment two revealed that Distrust influenced how the Ventral Striatum (VS) responded to feedback agreement.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2.

claim: Individuals with low distrust show strong agreement effect in VS for Target feedback, whereas individuals highly doubtful show comparable response for all Target feedback positions.
source: More specifically, whereas individuals with low distrust show strong agreement effect in this region, with enhanced activity whenever the Target's feedback coincides with their own judgment, individuals highly doubtful about the expression's authenticity show comparable response for all Target feedback positions (Figure 6B–C, yellow dots).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2 displayed in Figure 6.

claim: The effect of Distrust on VS did not generalize to the MPs' feedback, which exhibited the opposite trend.
source: Furthermore, this effect did not generalize to the MPs' feedback, which exhibited the opposite trend (violet dots).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 2 displayed in Figure 6.

claim: Distrust operates independently from the grouping factor and from the personal dispositions toward the category of doctors.
source: Furthermore, Distrust operates independently from the grouping factor and from the personal dispositions toward the category of doctors (measured through the IAT).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis showing Distrust effects are not confounded by group or IAT scores.

claim: Medical education leads to decreased sensitivity to others' pain both in terms of behavioral ratings and neural response of AI and dACC.
source: Overall, our data converge with, but also extend, previous evidence by showing that medical education leads to decreased sensitivity to others' pain (Cheng et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2007; Choinière et al., 1990; Davoudi et al., 2008), both in terms of behavioral ratings (when comparing EMS to YMS) and in the neural response of predefined regions such as AI and dACC (when comparing EMS to Controls).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from the study and relates them to previous literature.

claim: Distrust influences the processing of the feedbacks about one's pain assessment by inhibiting the neural processing implicated in treating information from the person in pain.
source: Our study provides a mechanistic explanation of these observations, by revealing that distrust operates on part of the network for feedback-based learning, and specifically by altering the sensitivity of the reward system to information from the person in pain.
evidence: This claim is based on the fMRI findings showing VS modulation by distrust.

claim: Confronting individuals from different social and ethnic group can impact representation of trust and associated activity in VS.
source: Previous studies showed that confronting individuals from different social and ethnic group can impact profoundly representation of trust and associated activity in VS (Hughes et al., 2017; Stanley et al., 2012; Stanley et al., 2011), but also sensitivity to their pain (Avenanti et al., 2010; Mende-Siedlecki et al., 2019) including the neural responses in AI and dACC (Cao et al., 2015; Hein et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The interplay between the reward system and AI-dACC network might offer a plausible model to explain why specific social/ethnic categories are less likely to be acknowledged for their pain and receive adequate treatment.
source: As such, the interplay between the reward system and AI-dACC network might offer a plausible model to explain why specific social/ethnic categories are less likely to be acknowledged for their pain and receive adequate treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the study's findings and previous literature.

claim: Experience in medical faculty influenced individuals' assessment of pain both at the level of explicit ratings and on a network comprehending insular and cingulate cortex.
source: Notwithstanding these considerations, our study provides compelling evidence of an independent contribution of experience and Distrust in different aspects of pain management. Experience in medical faculty influenced individuals' assessment of pain, both at the level of explicit ratings, and on a network comprehending insular and cingulate cortex knowingly sensitive to cues about people's suffering (Ding et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2011; Jauniaux et al., 2019; Kogler et al., 2020; Lamm et al., 2011; Timmers et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim summarizes the study's findings on experience effects.

claim: Distrust affected the processing of feedbacks about one's assessments by decreasing striatal activity whenever the Target's reports match participants' initial ratings.
source: Additionally, Distrust affected the processing of feedbacks about one's assessments, by decreasing striatal activity whenever the Target's reports match participants' initial ratings, and by leading participants to rely more on the opinion of other doctors.
evidence: This claim summarizes the study's findings on distrust effects.

claim: Distrust led participants to rely more on the opinion of other doctors.
source: Additionally, Distrust affected the processing of feedbacks about one's assessments, by decreasing striatal activity whenever the Target's reports match participants' initial ratings, and by leading participants to rely more on the opinion of other doctors.
evidence: This claim summarizes the study's findings on distrust effects.

claim: The study documents relevant changes in the neural circuity underling pain assessment and feedback processing that occur already at the very early stages of medical career.
source: Overall, our study documents relevant changes in the neural circuity underling pain assessment and feedback processing that occur already at the very early stages of medical career.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the study's overall findings.

claim: Experiment 1 recruited 120 participants organized in four groups of 30 subjects.
source: Because this was an exploratory experiment, we recruited an overall of 120 participants, organized in four groups of 30 subjects.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the study design.

claim: The pain of the video expressions was rated on average 7.42 ± 1.26 on a scale ranging from 1 to 10 in a validation pilot experiment.
source: A validation pilot experiment (Pilot 2) on 24 independent lay participants (seven males, age 23.54 ± 4.12) revealed that the pain of these expressions was rated on average 7.42 ± 1.26 on a scale ranging from 1 (no pain at all) to 10 (worst pain imaginable).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Pilot 2.

claim: The research was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: This research (both experiments) was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the local ethical committee (Commission Cantonale d'Éthique e de la Recherce [CCER] of Geneva, protocol code: CCER N. 2016–01862).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: The research was approved by the local ethical committee (Commission Cantonale d'Éthique e de la Recherce [CCER] of Geneva, protocol code: CCER N. 2016–01862).
source: This research (both experiments) was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the local ethical committee (Commission Cantonale d'Éthique e de la Recherce [CCER] of Geneva, protocol code: CCER N. 2016–01862).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.
